parts.title: Joining a Running Club
parts.context: A man who has recently moved to Australia phones a running club about becoming a member and entering its charity ten-kilometre race.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a running club to ask about joining the club and entering a race. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 4.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 1 to 4.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Wattle Bay Runners, Jodie speaking.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Oh, hello. Um, I got this number from your website. I'm thinking about joining the club, and I was also hoping to find out about the ten-kilometre race you're organising.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Lovely, you've come to the right person. I'm the club secretary, so I can help you with both. Can I grab your name first?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Ben. Ben Thursby. I've only just moved here from Manchester, so I don't really know anyone yet.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Well, a running club's a great way to fix that. Have you been running long?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: A few years, on and off. I did a couple of half marathons back home, but I've been a bit lazy since the move, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: No dramas. Right, so the club runs twice a week, Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and we start at six thirty.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: And where do you all meet? The website mentioned the library car park, I think.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Ah, yeah, sorry, the website's a bit out of date. We did use to meet at the library, but then the council started charging for parking there in the evenings. So these days we meet at the pavilion in Norfolk Park. It's the building right next to the cricket nets, you can't miss it.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The pavilion, next to the nets. Got it. And is there a membership fee?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: There is, it's an annual fee. It was sixty-five dollars last year, but we've had to put it up to seventy-two, mostly because our insurance went up.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Seventy-two. That's still very reasonable. Is there anything on top of that?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Only if you want a club singlet, and they're fifteen dollars. But that's entirely optional. Nobody makes you wear one to training.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Right... And what do I need to bring when I sign up? Do you need, um, a doctor's certificate or something? I know some clubs back in England ask for one.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: We used to, actually, but not any more. Now you just fill in a short health questionnaire on the night. What you will need to bring is a photo, because we print everyone a membership card, and the card gets you ten per cent off at the sports shop on the high street.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: A photo, fine, I can sort that out. Is there a group for people who are, er, getting back into it? I don't want to be left behind on my first night.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Everyone says that. Yes, there's a beginners' group on Tuesdays. It's run by one of our coaches, Gail Kerridge.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Sorry, was that Kerrigan?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: No, Kerridge. K... E... double R... I... D... G... E.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: K, E, double R, I, D, G, E. Thanks. And she always takes the beginners?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: She does now. She used to coach the juniors, but she swapped over this year, and honestly, she's brilliant with people who are nervous.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 5 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 5 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Now, the race. The charity ten K. When is it exactly? I saw a poster in a café that said the second of November.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Yeah, a lot of those posters went up before we had to change it. It was going to be Sunday the second, but the council's resurfacing the coast road that weekend, so we've moved it back a week. It's now Sunday the ninth.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The ninth of November. That actually suits me better. And where does it start? Somebody at work told me it starts at the surf club.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: It always has done, but the surf club's being rebuilt at the moment, so this year we're starting from the lighthouse, right at the north end of the beach. The finish is still in Norfolk Park, though, so it's a point-to-point course rather than a loop.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The lighthouse. That should be a nice view, at least. And how much does it cost to enter?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: That depends. For the general public it's forty-five dollars, but club members get a decent discount, so for members it's thirty.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Sorry, thirteen?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: I wish! No, thirty, three-oh. So if you join before you enter, you save fifteen dollars straight away.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Well, that's another good reason to join. And which charity does the money go to?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Last year it was the animal shelter, and the year before that it went to the surf lifesaving club. This year the committee voted for the local hospice. A few of our members have had family there, so it means a lot to people.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: That's a really good cause. And, er, how does it work on the day? Do I pick up my number at the start?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: That's how we used to do it, but the queues were terrible and people were missing the start. So now you collect your race pack the day before, on the Saturday, from the marina office, down by the boat ramp. It's open from nine till four.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The marina office. So nothing's given out on the Sunday morning?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Nothing at all, so don't leave it till the last minute. There is a bag drop at the lighthouse, though, and we drive all the bags back to the park for you.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Great. And is there anything for people who finish? A medal, or...?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Everyone gets a medal, yes. We used to hand out T-shirts as well, but to be honest, hardly anybody wore them, so this year every finisher gets a towel instead. A proper beach towel, with the race logo on it.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: A towel. That's actually useful, especially round here.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: That was the idea. Oh, and there are two water stations on the course, at three and seven kilometres, so you won't need to carry a bottle.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Brilliant. Right, I'll come along to the pavilion on Tuesday, then, and join properly.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Perfect. Don't forget your photo, and say hello to Gail. She'll look after you.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: I will. Thanks very much, Jodie. Bye.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Outdoor Education Week
parts.context: A primary school head teacher briefs parents at an evening meeting about the Year Six outdoor education week.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 2. You will hear a head teacher talking to parents about a school outdoor education week. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 14.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 11 to 14.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming out on such a wet night. I know some of you have come straight from work, so I'll try to keep this brisk. As you know, we're here to talk about the Year Six outdoor education week, which takes place in the first week of June.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Some of you will remember that when the school first started these trips, about ten years ago, the main idea was simply to get children more active. And fitness is still a very welcome side effect, of course. Other parents have said to me that it's a useful step towards secondary school, and I'd agree that it helps with that.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: But what the staff and I really want from the week this year is for the children to learn to manage without us. To pack their own bags, keep track of their own kit, and make decisions in their groups without an adult jumping in to sort everything out. That's harder than it sounds, for them and for us.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Now, some practical details. We're going back to Brackenside, the centre in mid-Wales that we used last year, so a lot of the staff already know the site well. The children will again be in activity groups of eight, each with its own instructor. We did ask whether the groups could be cut to six, but the centre simply couldn't staff that.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: What has changed is that, rather than coming home on the Wednesday as they did last year, the children will stay a second night and come back on the Thursday afternoon. The feedback we had was that one night was over almost before it had begun.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: The cost this year is two hundred and ten pounds. I know several families asked whether there's a reduction when brothers and sisters, or twins, go together. I'm afraid the centre doesn't offer one. The coach isn't part of that figure, either. The parents' association has very generously agreed to pay for it this year.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: What we can do is let you split the payment into three equal parts, in March, April and May, rather than paying it all at once. Just let the office know which you'd prefer. And if the cost is a real difficulty for any family, please come and talk to me privately. Nobody will miss out for that reason.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Mobile phones. Last year, as some of you will recall, we let the children bring them. They were collected when we arrived and handed back for half an hour each evening. Honestly, it caused far more homesickness than it cured. So this year, please don't pack a phone at all. If you need to reach your child, ring the centre, and we'll put photos on the school blog every evening.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 15 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 15 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Let me run through the activities now, because each one needs something slightly different from you. On the first full day there's cycling, in the morning. Helmets and bikes are provided by the centre, and the children will be back in plenty of time for lunch. However, part of the route goes along a quiet public lane, so this is the one activity the centre won't let a child take part in without your signature on the permission slip.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Then canoeing, on the lake. Everyone is given a wetsuit and a buoyancy aid, so they don't need extra clothes for that. But their feet will get soaked, without exception, so they'll need a second pair of trainers or old shoes to change into afterwards, otherwise they'll be squelching about all day.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: The pond and stream study comes next. Some parents asked if the children should bring a torch, for looking under rocks and so on. They don't need one. What I would say is that the mud at Brackenside is a peculiar shade of orange, and it does not wash out. Please send them in something old that you won't mind putting straight in the bin afterwards.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: On the second evening, there's a night walk up through the woods, which the children always love. The centre used to lend out lamps for this, but they've stopped doing that now. So every child must bring a torch of their own. It doesn't need to be anything fancy, and please, not one that flashes.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: The orienteering day is the longest one. The groups are out in Gwern Forest from morning until late afternoon, which is too far to come back to the centre, so for once the kitchen won't be providing a hot lunch. Please make sure your child has sandwiches and a drink with them that morning. You might think they'd need sun cream, being out all day, but the centre has huge supplies, so please don't send any.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: And finally, climbing, on the indoor wall. The children's harnesses are all checked by the instructors, so you needn't worry about equipment. But the climbing centre insists, and this is their rule rather than ours, on having a list of any medicines a child takes, especially inhalers, before that session. If that applies to your child, please write it on the form that's going home tonight.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: One last thing. There's a small shop at Brackenside, and in the past children have taken pocket money. This year the shop will be closed for refurbishment, so they won't need any money at all. Right, I'll stop there. Are there any questions?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Commuting Survey Data
parts.context: Two postgraduate students discuss the results of their survey into how people in the city commute and use public transport.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 3. You will hear two postgraduate students, Niamh and Marcus, discussing the results of a survey they carried out on commuting and public transport. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 25.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 21 to 25.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Right, Niamh, I've finally got all the responses into one spreadsheet. Four hundred and twelve in total.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Not bad at all. Fewer than we hoped, mind you. I think the questionnaire was just too long. Twelve pages was asking a lot of people. So, where did most of them come from in the end? Online?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: That's what I assumed too, given how much we pushed the link on social media. But no, the online version only got about a hundred and thirty. The paper copies did far better, and nearly all of those came from libraries.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Really? Not the doctors' surgeries?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: We got a grand total of nineteen from the surgeries. And the supermarkets wouldn't let us leave any in the first place, if you remember.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Oh yes, I remember the manager's face. And to think we spent a whole weekend designing that online version. Still, at least the paper ones were properly filled in. Half the online people gave up after page three.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Yeah, the completion rate on paper was much better. Anyway.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: OK. So, the big question. Why do the drivers say they don't use the buses? I'd have bet money it'd be the fares.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: So would I. But cost only came third. It isn't the price that puts them off, and it isn't really the journey time, which was second. By some distance, the thing drivers kept coming back to was reliability. Buses not turning up, or two arriving at once.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: That fits with the comments section, actually. People were furious about the number seven route. What about the cyclists? I was expecting pages about dangerous traffic.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: There was some of that, and a fair few mentioned showers at work. But the real complaint wasn't safety on the roads at all. It was that there's nowhere to leave a bike. They want secure storage, at the station and at work, because so many of them have had bikes stolen.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Right. And the over-sixties? I suppose price doesn't matter much to them, since most of them travel free.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Exactly, cost hardly featured. And interestingly, speed wasn't a big deal either. When we asked them to rank things, they put comfort above journey time almost every time. Getting a seat, a smooth ride, that sort of thing. Which surprised me a bit, actually. I'd assumed reliability would top their list as well, the same as it did for the drivers, but it only came third for them.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: That's a nice finding. Now, presentation. Doctor Ellis said tables, didn't she?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: She did say tables were fine for the appendix. And I'd started doing bar charts for everything.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: But so much of this is about where people live. I really think the main findings should go on maps. You'd see the gaps in the bus network straight away.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Yeah... you're right. Maps for the main results, then. I'll ditch the bar charts.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 26 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 26 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: We need to be honest about the sample, though. Doctor Ellis will go straight for it.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: I know. My worry's the young people. I thought we'd hardly have any under twenty-five.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: We're actually fine there, they're about twenty-two per cent, which is close to the city as a whole. And before you say it, students aren't a problem either. There were only about forty of them.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: No, you're right. The thing that does bother me is the postcodes. Nearly two thirds of the responses are from the eastern side of the city, because that's where the libraries we used are.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: That's the real weakness, isn't it? We can't say much about the west at all.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Agreed. What about the working-from-home question? A lot of people have said that's the most surprising part of the data.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: I don't think it surprised anyone, to be honest. It's what every report's been saying for years. My problem with it is the wording. We asked how often people work remotely, and half of them didn't know whether to count a morning at home as a day or not. You can see they've interpreted it in completely different ways.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Would it have helped if it had come earlier, before people got tired?

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: I don't think where it was made any difference. It's the way we phrased it.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Fair enough. Now, the follow-up interviews. You know I was against putting them in at first.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: You said eight interviews weren't worth the paper.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: I did. And it wasn't Doctor Ellis who changed my mind, either, although she did suggest them. And they certainly don't fix the response rate, eight people isn't going to do that. It's that they make sense of those odd figures for the occasional bus users, the ones who say they hate the buses and use them anyway. The interviews show why.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Great, so they're in. And the national census figures? I'd love to use them to back up our main argument.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: The trouble is their categories don't match ours. They lump cycling and walking together, for one thing. And they're from four years ago, before all the changes to the bus routes, so any comparison would be a bit misleading.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Hmm. I don't want to bin them completely, though. They took ages to find.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: How about we stick them at the back, as supporting material, but don't build anything on them?

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: OK, an appendix it is. So, before we see Doctor Ellis on Friday... should we email the bus company for their passenger numbers?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: They'd take weeks to reply. And there's no time to set up more interviews either.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Then let's go back through the written comments. I noticed we've coded some of them differently from each other, so we should sort that out first.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Good idea. I'll take the first half, you take the second, and we can compare notes on Thursday evening. Then at least we'll walk in on Friday agreeing with each other.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: How Suspension Bridges Carry Loads
parts.context: An engineering lecturer explains how suspension bridges are built, how they carry loads, and the problems caused by wind, pedestrians and corrosion.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the engineering of suspension bridges. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Okay, let's get started. Today we're looking at suspension bridges, which, for the longest spans, are still pretty much the only option we have. I want to focus on how they actually carry loads, and then on what can go wrong.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Just to put that in context: a good concrete beam bridge might span a couple of hundred meters between supports, and a cable-stayed bridge perhaps a thousand. The longest suspension bridges now cross more than two kilometers in a single span. So whatever they're doing, they're doing it very efficiently, and the reason comes down to how each part shares the work.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The basic idea is simple. The deck, the part you drive on, hangs from vertical cables, and those vertical cables hang from two main cables that run over the tops of the towers. Now, a lot of students assume the main cables are being squeezed by all that weight. They aren't. A cable can't resist being squeezed at all. The main cables are only ever in tension. They're being pulled. It's the towers that work in compression, pushing the load straight down into the foundations.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So where does the pull in the cables end up? At each end of the bridge, the cables are tied into anchorages. These are enormous blocks, and their whole job is to be heavy enough not to be dragged toward the river. On older bridges, they were built of masonry, cut stone, and in a few places the cables were simply anchored into solid rock. But today, almost without exception, anchorages are made of concrete, sometimes hundreds of thousands of tons of it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The main cables themselves are fascinating. You might picture a giant twisted rope, like a ship's hawser. That's not how it's done. Each cable is made of thousands of thin, parallel steel wires, and they're laid in place one at a time, high above the water, by a wheel running backward and forward between the anchorages. The process looks a bit like weaving, but engineers call it spinning, and it can take more than a year.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's think about the shape of the cable. If you hang a chain between two points, with nothing attached, it forms a curve called a catenary. You'll see that word in older textbooks applied to bridges. But a suspension bridge cable isn't just hanging under its own weight. Once the deck is attached, and the load is spread evenly along the span, the curve is much closer to a parabola. And that's the shape designers actually work with.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Here's a detail I love. On the very longest bridges, the towers aren't exactly parallel. They're a few centimeters farther apart at the top than at the bottom. It's not a construction error, and it's not the cables pulling them outward either. It's because each tower points toward the center of the Earth, so the curvature of the planet means they lean very slightly away from each other.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, what can go wrong? The big enemy is wind. You've probably all seen the film of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in nineteen forty, twisting until it fell apart. You'll often read that it was destroyed by resonance, like a singer shattering a glass. That's not really accurate. Engineers now agree the cause was flutter, a self-feeding twisting motion, where the movement of the deck changes the airflow, which then makes the movement bigger.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: After Tacoma, the first response was to make decks far stiffer. Designers didn't change the shape much at first. Instead, they hung deep trusses underneath the road, a kind of open steel framework, which stopped the deck from twisting. Later, especially in Europe, engineers went the other way, with slim box decks shaped rather like an aircraft wing, which they test in wind tunnels before anything is built. Both approaches work, but the wing-shaped decks use far less steel.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Wind isn't the only problem, though. People can be one too. When London's Millennium Bridge opened in two thousand, which is a very shallow suspension bridge, it started swaying from side to side. Pedestrians unconsciously fell into step with the movement, which made it worse. The bridge was closed, and there was talk of closing it for good, or rebuilding it entirely. In the end, the fix was to install dampers, devices that absorb the energy of the motion, a bit like the shock absorbers in a car.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, maintenance. You might expect the biggest long-term worry to be metal fatigue, the gradual weakening from millions of loading cycles. In fact, for main cables, that's a relatively minor issue. The real threat is corrosion. Water gets in between the wires, and once they start to rust, they snap, one at a time, deep inside the cable where nobody can see them.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So how do you find a broken wire you can't see? One method is to unwrap sections of cable and inspect them by eye, but that's slow and very expensive. X-rays have been tried, but the cables are just too thick. What many bridges use now is acoustic monitoring. Microphones are clamped along the cable, and when a wire breaks, it gives off a sharp crack, and the system records exactly where and when it happened.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Some bridges go further and blow dry air through the cables to stop corrosion before it starts, and we'll look at those systems next week. For now, I'd like you to read the case study on the reading list before Thursday.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.
